Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Authority Figures: People in uniform, Military Topics: Talks about military, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Carry Weapon: carry weapon, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Vignette:
Seventy-year-old Latin American male, Dr. Jorge Perez, is a retired dentist who has been struggling with intrusive memories and distressing emotions since a terrorist attack that took place three years ago in his city. The traumatic event occurred while he was attending a community health fair, where he volunteered to provide free dental check-ups for underprivileged families. On that fateful day, terrorists detonated several bombs at the venue, causing widespread panic, injuries, and fatalities. Dr. Perez vividly remembers the chaos as the explosions echoed through the air, followed by the sharp, alarming sound of gunfire. He was certain that he could hear gunshots even though they might have been just echoes of his own heartbeat pounding in his ears. The memory of the blasts and the accompanying sounds have left him on high alert whenever he hears unexpected or loud noises. This has made it particularly difficult for him to attend any large gatherings, especially those involving authority figures in uniform. Since then, Dr. Perez has developed a range of avoidance behaviors that have gradually altered his daily routine. He now carries a concealed weapon with him wherever he goes, believing it offers some measure of protection against potential threats. This habit emerged as a coping mechanism to deal with his heightened sense of vulnerability and the constant fear that another attack might happen at any moment. Dr. Perez is also extremely wary of news reports about events similar to what happened in his city. He has grown accustomed to avoiding media coverage altogether, fearing that it would bring back the overwhelming emotions associated with the trauma. This avoidance extends to conversations about military topics and people in uniform. When he encounters these triggers, whether on TV or in real life, he experiences intense anxiety and a sense of dread. The traumatic event is deeply ingrained in Dr. Perez's mind, but he finds it incredibly difficult to articulate his feelings and thoughts about what happened. He can't seem to put the frightening event into words, which has left him feeling isolated and unable to share his struggles with others. When memories resurface, they are so overwhelming that he must stop whatever he is doing until the intensity subsides. The full sensory reliving of the event—seeing the chaos, hearing the blasts, and feeling the terror—leaves him shaken and drained. In addition to these symptoms, Dr. Perez often scans for exits as soon as he enters any room or building. He watches other people closely for signs that they might harm him, a constant state of hypervigilance that has made social interactions extremely challenging. His heightened sense of threat has also affected his ability to engage in daily activities and maintain relationships with friends and neighbors. As a dentist, Dr. Perez’s profession once brought him immense satisfaction and pride, but now he finds it difficult to concentrate on even routine tasks. The stress and anxiety have taken their toll, leading to frequent cancellations of appointments and declining performance at work. His colleagues and patients have noticed the change in his demeanor, which has strained his professional relationships. What frightened Dr. Perez most was the feeling that he could have prevented or mitigated the tragedy if he had acted differently. He repeatedly blames himself for what happened, ruminating over thoughts of how things might have been different if only he had made different choices on that day. This self-blame has left him with a profound sense of guilt and an overwhelming need to protect himself from any future harm. Ultimately, it was the growing realization that his life was becoming increasingly unmanageable that prompted Dr. Perez to seek help. He is most afraid of never being able to reclaim a sense of normalcy or peace. At the same time, he hopes for a way to cope with his memories and fears so that he can resume a fulfilling life without constant dread and anxiety.
